We need retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction. The target SMILES includes a fluorinated carbon (CF3) attached to a carbon bearing the ring and OH? Let's decode: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

So it's a bicyclic? Actually it's a cyclopentanol fused? The fragment: C@@H1CCCC1O is a cyclopentanol. That carbon (C@@H9) attached to the alkene carbon (C2) and to the cyclopentane ring. The alkene is exocyclic CH2= C(aryl)(C*). So the forward carbonyl-ene reaction: starting from a ketone and an alkene that undergo intramolecular ene to give this product. So retrosynthesis: break the C-O bond (hydroxyl) to a carbonyl (ketone) and break the C-C bond formed between the alkene carbon and the cyclopentane carbon, generating a C=C double bond and a carbonyl. So precursor would be a molecule with a ketone at that carbon (C13?) and an alkene CH2= C(aryl) attached to same carbon? Actually the product has a new C-C bond between C2 (alkene carbon) and C9 (the carbon bearing OH). In the forward ene, the alkene (CH2= C(aryl) ) reacts with allylic hydrogen on cyclopentanol precursor (which had a carbonyl). The allylic hydrogen is on the carbon adjacent to carbonyl? In typical carbonyl-ene, carbonyl acts as ene acceptor, alkene as ene donor, forming new C-C bond between alkene carbon and allylic carbon, and moving hydrogen to carbonyl oxygen forming OH. So precursor likely is a cyclopentanone (five-membered ring with carbonyl) attached to the same carbon (C9) that will become the allylic carbon. The alkene part is same: CH2= C(aryl). So precursor SMILES: [CH2]=[C]([c1ccccc1])C1CCCC(=O)C(F)(F)F? Wait the CF3 attached to same carbon as carbonyl? In product, CF3 attached to C15 which is same carbon as carbonyl carbon? Actually product: C@@:13 ([OH]) [C:15]([F])([F])([F]) . So carbon 13 is chiral carbon bearing OH and attached to CF3 carbon (C15). In precursor, carbonyl carbon would be C15 (C=O) attached to C13 (which is carbon bearing CF3?). Let's think: In product, there is a carbon bearing OH (C13) and attached to CF3 carbon (C15) via a single bond. The CF3 carbon is attached to C13 and maybe also to something else? In product, C15 is attached to C13, three Fs, and maybe nothing else (makes CF3). So precursor would have carbonyl at C15 (C=O) attached to C13 (which is the allylic carbon). So precursor SMILES: [CH2]=[C]([c1ccccc1])C1CCCC1C(=O)C(F)(F)F? Wait the carbonyl carbon is attached to C13 which is part of cyclopentane ring. So cyclopentanone with CF3 substituent at carbonyl carbon? Actually carbonyl carbon is part of CF3 carbon? No carbonyl carbon is C15, which in product is CF3 carbon (sp3). So in precursor, C15 is carbonyl carbon (C=O) attached to CF3? But CF3 can't be attached to carbonyl carbon; carbonyl carbon is double bonded to O, and also attached to CF3 group? That would be a trifluoroacetyl group (CF3-CO-). So precursor could be a trifluoroacetyl group attached to the cyclopentane carbon (C13). So structure: cyclopentane bearing a CF3-CO group (trifluoroacetyl) at carbon 13, and also attached to alkene CH2=C(aryl). So the precursor SMILES: [CH2]=[C]([c1ccccc1])C1CCCC1C(=O)C(F)(F)F . That seems plausible.

Thus retrosynthetic step: apply carbonyl-ene reverse (i.e., break C-O and C-C, form C=O and C=C). So we need a template for carbonyl-ene reaction. Let's search for template with functional groups broken: ketone, C-C double bonds; formed: aliphatic hydroxyl, five-membered rings. Use correct functional group names: "ketones", "C-C double bonds" are valid. For formed: "aliphatic hydroxyls", "five-membered rings". Use those.
